title: The yeast of the Pharisees (Matthew 16:1–12)
hook: one sour comment turns a whole group chat: how small things spread
tomorrow: who do people say you are, and who do you say you are?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother who kept asking until she heard: great is your faith. Today, something small that won't stay small.

One sour comment lands in the group chat, and ten messages later the whole thread has turned. Nobody decided that. It spread. Bakers know how: a pinch of starter worked into a new batch, and the whole dough rises. Jesus uses that picture in a boat. He's just crossed the lake with his friends, and partway over, someone realizes the problem. They forgot to bring bread.
screen: `ONE SOUR COMMENT.` → `A PINCH OF STARTER.` → `THEY FORGOT THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Into that worried boat, Jesus says: "Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees." The disciples hear bread, only bread: "It is because we have taken no bread." He reminds them of the loaves and the baskets, two crowds just fed, and then it clicks: "Then understood they how that he bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees." A teaching, working its way through a person. And leaven itself isn't the villain: by the lake, he said the kingdom of heaven is like leaven too. Paul puts it in one line: "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump." So the question is how small things spread in a heart, and the answer is: quietly, and all the way through. A neighbor tradition knows this picture well. Before Passover, Jewish tradition clears the home of leaven, chametz, as the Torah commands. And in the Talmud, a teacher named Rabbi Alexandri ends his prayer by asking what keeps us from doing God's will, and his answer includes the yeast in the dough. Shared ground: yeast as what quietly works its way through. The honest difference: Matthew's leaven is a teaching to beware of; in the Talmud's prayer, the yeast is a pull inside a person. And in Jewish life, bread isn't bad the rest of the year. The clearing belongs to Passover.
screen: `BEWARE THE LEAVEN.` · `NOT BREAD, BUT A TEACHING.` · `A NEIGHBOR: CLEARING THE CHAMETZ.` · `THE YEAST IN THE DOUGH.`

segments.voice: Catch one sour thought you've carried today, and name it once, plainly. Then count three small good things on your fingers, slowly, letting each one settle before the next. A little leaven works both ways.
The yeast of the Pharisees. Jesus' picture, in Matthew 16, for a teaching that works its way through a person the way leaven works through dough.

chat.meaning: Jewish tradition clears leaven for Passover; Jesus warns of the leaven of a teaching (16:12). A shared picture, used differently.

leaven.meaning: yeast or sourdough starter that makes dough rise

Sadducees.meaning: a group of Jewish leaders tied to the temple

Passover.meaning: the Jewish festival remembering freedom from slavery in Egypt

chametz.meaning: leavened food, cleared from Jewish homes for Passover

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' recorded discussions of Jewish law and life

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): Passover's clearing of leaven (Exodus 12:15, paraphrased) and Rabbi Alexandri's prayer naming 'the yeast in the dough' (Berakhot 17a, paraphrased) are set beside Matthew 16. Shared ground: yeast as what quietly spreads. Honest difference: Matthew names a teaching; the Talmud's prayer names a pull within a person (Rashi reads it as the evil inclination; not stated in the voice); and for Jews bread is ordinary food outside Passover. Please have a Jewish reviewer confirm the attribution, the paraphrase and that nothing is ranked.
The index carry 'a little leaven' comes from Paul (Galatians 5:9; 1 Corinthians 5:6 has nearly the same words), not from Matthew 16; the voice credits it to Paul.

Framing: the warning is presented as Matthew presents it (16:12, the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees), with leaven shown to be a neutral image (13:33); the disciples' own worry is the example of leaven at work. The Pharisees are not made the foil. Confirm.
The red-sky saying (16:2–3), which some ancient manuscripts lack, is left out of this version.

howItsDone: the search for leaven the night before Passover (bedikat chametz) is hedged with 'some Jewish families'; communion bread practice differs among churches and is stated without ranking. Confirm.
